evidence.title: Fed Raises Rates In Fight To Tame Inflation
evidence.body: [e001:f01] The Fed's rate hike aims to control inflation but raises borrowing costs, which is expected to impact real estate and economic growth. [e001:f02] First Rate Hike Since 2023 Lands Atop 5% Treasury Yield, Ratcheting Up Capital Pressure September 16, 2026 | 2:05 pm ET Matt Wasielewski, National Federal Open Market Committee members voted unanimously Wednesday to raise the Federal Reserve 's benchmark rate, an expected but significant shift in the central bank’s fight to tame inflation. [e001:f03] The decision is the first rate increase since July 2023 and ends a five-meeting string of votes to hold rates flat. [e001:f04] Investors started the year confident that the path forward from the FOMC in 2026 would be rate cuts, but stubbornly elevated inflation shifted expectations and forced the Fed to go the opposite route. [e001:f05] “Cap rate movement is unlikely to be unilateral — market by market, sector by sector — but certainly a trend toward higher capital costs will impact transactional volume.” In its statement released with the decision, the Fed said the economy remains relatively robust despite elevated uncertainty, and the central bank was clear that the move to raise rates was meant to target the pace of price hikes. [e001:f06] “Interest Rates in the United States should be 1% or less because we are the Best Credit in the World,” he wrote. [e001:f07] The central bank is tasked with price stability and maximum employment, and the move to raise the benchmark rate to a range between 3.75% and 4% represents its most aggressive attempt in years to tamp down inflation. [e001:f08] But the rate hike comes as investors already face a challenging debt environment, with yields on 10-year Treasury bonds surpassing the 5% mark and pushing up borrowing costs at the same time that delinquency rates are climbing . [e001:f09] “The impact of the recent rate increase will likely tame enthusiasm for any marginal development projects and could elevate capitalization rates,” Noel Liston , managing broker at Core Industrial Realty, said via email. [e001:f10] “However, the rate increase reinforces the Fed’s commitment to tame inflation and longer-term bond yields may not increase much if the market believes the pain of higher rates will be shorter in nature.” Yields on 10-year Treasury bonds jumped during Warsh’s press conference Wednesday and ended the day just above 5%. [e001:f11] Projections also moved toward a tighter labor market and a narrower expected range for inflation this year, coalescing around a 3.75% midpoint and staying above 3% across 2027. [e001:f12] Flickr/Federalreserve Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh and Governors Philip Jefferson and Michelle Bowman Wednesday’s decision to raise rates was expected, and the financial projections indicate another 25 bps hike is likely this year, Michael Pearce, chief U.S. economist at Oxford Economics, said in an email. [e001:f13] “We don’t think this is the beginning of another major tightening cycle and markets have too much tightening priced in over the coming year.” The consumer price index recorded 3.4% annualized inflation in August, up by 0.4% from the prior month and far from the central bank’s longtime 2% target. [e001:f14] The central bank opted to hold rates flat in Warsh’s first two meetings at the helm, but there were signs that a hike may be on the horizon. [e001:f15] Three FOMC members dissented in July in favor of a 25 bps hike, and Wednesday’s decision could help bolster the Fed’s independence after unprecedented interventions from the White House. [e001:f16] “The increase reinforced that the Fed remains focused on inflation, and is willing to maintain restrictive policy even as higher borrowing costs weigh on rate-sensitive sectors,” Andrew Koller, research analyst at Wolf Commercial Real Estate / CORFAC International , said in an email.
